title: Same Face, Different Inside: The Lanthanoids
subject: Chemistry
objective: The lanthanoids (lanthanum and the fourteen elements after it) have the general configuration [Xe] 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s². Each new electron goes into the deep 4f subshell, shielded by 5s²5p⁶, while the outer 6s² stays the same, so the elements are very alike (the Ytterby minerals took chemists over a century to sort out). Losing 6s² and one more electron gives the characteristic +3 state (La³⁺ 4f⁰ … Lu³⁺ 4f¹⁴). +4 and +2 appear near empty, half-filled or full 4f (Ce⁴⁺ 4f⁰, Tb⁴⁺ 4f⁷, Eu²⁺ 4f⁷, Yb²⁺ 4f¹⁴), but Ce⁴⁺ is a strong oxidant and Eu²⁺ a strong reductant: both return to +3.

fill.q: The lanthanoids are lanthanum and the ____ elements that follow it.

tf.q: The 4f electrons are shielded by the 5s and 5p electrons.
Eu²⁺ is a strong oxidising agent.
tf.explain: It is a strong reducing agent.

tf.q: Lanthanoids are placed in a separate row of the periodic table.
Yb²⁺ has a completely filled 4f subshell.

ar.a: +3 is the most common oxidation state of lanthanoids.
ar.r: The energy to remove 6s² and one more electron is repaid by hydration/lattice energy of Ln³⁺.

ar.a: Eu²⁺ is a strong reducing agent.
ar.r: Eu²⁺ readily loses an electron to reach the common +3 state.

short.q: Give the general electronic configuration of the lanthanoids with two examples.
Why do Ce⁴⁺ and Eu²⁺ exist, and why do they revert to +3?
short.solution: They reach special configurations (Ce⁴⁺ 4f⁰, Eu²⁺ 4f⁷), but +3 is energetically preferred; Ce⁴⁺ is therefore a strong oxidant and Eu²⁺ a strong reductant.

short.q: Why are lanthanoids difficult to separate from one another?
short.solution: Successive electrons enter the inner 4f subshell (shielded by 5s²5p⁶); the outer configuration and ionic sizes are almost the same, so their chemistry is nearly identical.
